title: FRM Operational, Lesson 9: The seven Basel event types and internal loss data
subtitle: If you cannot classify an event you cannot build a loss distribution - and you cannot compute capital
whyItMatters: Every operational risk model starts from a loss database classified consistently. Ad hoc classification makes years of data useless, because it cannot be compared across business units and cannot be pooled with industry data.
openingQuestion: Why does Basel define seven operational risk event types in advance rather than letting each bank classify for itself?
openingOptions: So that loss data can be compared and pooled
So that banks have fewer events to record in the tracking log
So that the regulator can apply the same penalty to every event type
So that banks need not retain loss data for more than three years
explanation: A single bank's internal data is usually far too sparse in the tail - the events that are rare but do the most damage. Supplementing it with industry data requires classifying to the same standard, otherwise your number and someone else's are describing two different things.

diagram.label: An event occurs → record it in the loss database
Assign the Basel event type and the business line
Pool with industry data to fill the missing tail
Build the frequency and severity distributions → compute capital

realWorldExample.company: Why internal loss data is always thin in the tail
realWorldExample.description: A bank may record thousands of small events each year - keying errors, settlement mistakes - but meets a truly catastrophic event once in several decades, or never. It is precisely that rare region which drives most of the capital requirement. This is why industry loss data consortia came into being, and why expert scenario analysis is used to fill in for data that will never be sufficient.

quiz.question: Why does every loss event need both an event type and a business line assigned to it?
options: Because the business line decides whether it is operational risk at all
Because the reporting system only accepts exactly two fields
Because a two-way tag halves the number of events to record
Because capital is computed on an event-type × business-line matrix
quiz.explanation: Internal fraud on a proprietary trading desk carries a completely different potential severity from internal fraud in the retail business. The two-way matrix preserves that information rather than collapsing everything into a single number. Neither tag decides whether an event is operational at all - that follows from the root cause - and tagging adds work rather than reducing it: the number of events to record is set by the reporting threshold, not by how many fields each one carries.

quiz.question: What does setting the loss recording threshold too high do to the model?
options: The body of the loss distribution gets cut away
The model then produces a higher capital requirement
Large loss events go missing from the dataset entirely
The bank no longer classifies by Basel event type
quiz.explanation: A high threshold removes the small and medium events - by far the most numerous part of the data. Frequency estimated on what remains comes out lower than reality, and fitting a distribution to truncated data requires its own correction technique if the parameters are not to be biased. Large events are the ones a high threshold definitely still captures, which is what makes the damage easy to miss: nothing looks absent, and the capital number typically falls rather than rises because the frequency estimate has collapsed.

quiz.question: Why should near misses be recorded even though no financial loss occurred?
options: Because Basel requires capital for events that caused no loss
Because they reveal a real control gap that got lucky this time
Because more data points make the model statistically sharper
Because they are recorded as exceptional income in the annual accounts
quiz.explanation: A mistaken transfer caught in time before it left the system costs nothing at all, but the gap that allowed it remains exactly where it was. The value of this data is preventive rather than capital-related, which is why it is held outside the loss distribution: feeding zero-severity events into a severity model would distort it rather than sharpen it, no capital is charged against them, and nothing is recognised in the accounts because no money moved.

quiz.question: Why does external loss data have to be scaled before it is used?
options: Because other firms classify events under a standard other than Basel
Because external data is always published several years behind
Because a loss at a far larger firm does not scale to yours
Because another firm's loss is outside your capital model
quiz.explanation: A payment system failure costing a trillion at a bank twenty times your size does not mean you would take the same hit. Without scaling, the tail of the distribution is inflated and so is the capital you must set aside. The point of the seven Basel event types is precisely that firms sharing data classify the same way, so the standard is not the obstacle, and external losses are brought into your model deliberately - the question is how much of each one applies at your scale.

quiz.question: How does Basel handle the boundary between operational risk and credit risk?
options: The boundary is set by each firm in its own internal policy
Every loss with a human error element counts as operational risk
A loss between the two types is split by estimated proportion
A loss from a faulty credit file stays credit risk but is still logged
quiz.explanation: This is the classic boundary case: the loan lost money, so for capital purposes it is a credit loss, but the cause was a process failure, so it must sit in the operational data where the model can see it. Dropping it from either place distorts the picture. Note that this is a prescribed treatment rather than a matter of internal policy, and that splitting the amount across both types would be the one answer that double counts nothing but measures neither.

practicePrompt.question: A bank sets its operational loss recording threshold at 500m dong to cut data entry volume. What follows for the model?
options: The body of the distribution is lost, so frequency comes out biased
No effect, because capital is decided by the tail alone
The model runs faster and estimates more stably than before
Only small events are lost, and they have no analytical value
practicePrompt.explanation: An operational loss distribution has a great many small events and very few large ones, so a high threshold cuts away the most populous part of the data. Two consequences travel together: estimated frequency comes out below reality because most events go uncounted, and the distribution shape fitted to a truncated sample no longer describes the population - including the tail, since the parameters are estimated from the whole sample. Small events have their own value too: they repeat often enough to show which process is failing, before a large event happens in that same place.

keyTakeaways: The seven Basel event types exist so that data can be compared and pooled across institutions
Every event carries two tags: the event type and the business line
A recording threshold set too high cuts away the body of the distribution and biases the estimate
Near misses carry no capital charge but have high preventive value

summary.keyIdea: The quality of every operational risk model is capped by the quality and consistency of the loss database
summary.commonMistake: Setting a high recording threshold to reduce workload, then fitting a distribution to the truncated data without correcting for it
summary.action: When you look at a loss database, check the recording threshold and the consistency of the tagging before trusting any number in it

application.title: Spot the operational risk events around you
application.message: At whatever organisation you work in, try listing three recent process incidents and assigning them yourself to the seven Basel types. Most will land in execution, delivery and process management.
application.secondary: That is also the group with the largest count but the smallest value per case at most institutions.

sections.text: Operational risk is hard to measure because it has no price variable to track the way market risk does. What stands in its place is loss data - and data is only usable when it is classified consistently.

items: Internal fraud: deliberate acts by someone inside the organisation
External fraud: theft and cyber attack from outside
Clients, products and business practices: mis-selling, breaches of duty to clients
Damage to physical assets: natural disaster, fire
Execution, delivery and process management: keying errors, settlement mistakes, documentation failures

sections.text: Every event is assigned an event type and a business line at the same time. The reason is that the potential severity of the same event type varies enormously across business lines: internal fraud on a proprietary desk can bring down the whole bank, while in retail it usually stops at a far smaller scale.

sections.label: The recording threshold problem
sections.text: Recording every single event however small is impossible on cost grounds, so institutions set a threshold. But a threshold set high cuts away the body of the distribution, making the frequency estimate artificially low and biasing the fitted parameters unless a correction technique for truncated data is used.

lines: Loss data is the foundation of every operational risk model, and that foundation is poured with classification discipline.
Next lesson: when historical data is not enough, the institution assesses its own risks and controls.
